intro.html: Some people bow too low; others stand too tall. This topic gives you words for both ends: the flatterers who will say anything to please someone powerful, and the bold ones who say whatever they like, no matter who is listening.

Bowing: deferential (politely respectful, a good thing), then obsequious, servile and fawning (too eager to please), and the sycophant who flatters to get ahead. Standing too tall: insolent, impudent, brazen, and the nouns temerity and effrontery (nerve).
Good manners sit in the middle. Being deferential to a grandparent is kind; being obsequious to a boss is embarrassing; being insolent to anyone is rude.

words.def: showing polite respect and readiness to give way to others
words.ex: The young players were {deferential} to their coach, listening closely and never interrupting.
words.ctx: Though he outranked everyone on board, the new captain was {deferential}, asking the older sailors for advice before giving a single order.
words.etym: From deference, from defer (to yield to another person’s wishes), from Latin deferre (to carry down, to hand over).

mn.text: At the door, Dev steps back, bows a little and lets Granny Mae go first; showing her that polite respect is being {deferential}.

scene.alt: A teen bows slightly and holds back so his grandmother can walk through the door first.

words.def: too eager to please or obey someone
words.ex: The {obsequious} waiter refilled our glasses every thirty seconds and laughed at every joke.
words.ctx: A helpful assistant is a gift, but Victor was {obsequious}: he bowed whenever the boss walked by, agreed with everything she said and even held an umbrella over her on sunny days.
words.etym: From Latin obsequiosus, “compliant,” from obsequi (to comply): ob- (toward) + sequi (to follow).

mn.text: Victor follows the queen everywhere, bowing low and crying, “Anything, Your Majesty! Anything!” That much eagerness to please is {obsequious}.

scene.alt: A man bows low and follows a bored queen, holding an umbrella over her indoors.

words.def: a person who flatters powerful people to get ahead
words.ex: The king’s court was crowded with {sycophants} who praised every word he said.
words.ctx: Instead of warning the boss that her plan had serious problems, the {sycophant} praised it loudly, hoping to win the promotion.
words.etym: From Greek sykophantes, literally “one who shows the fig”; no one is sure how it came to mean a flatterer.

mn.text: Rex follows the champion around shouting, “You’re the GREATEST! Can I carry your trophy?” He does it only to win favors; he is a {sycophant}.

scene.alt: A flatterer waves a sign and shouts praise at a champion holding a trophy.

words.def: too willing to serve or obey others
words.ex: The {servile} assistant agreed with every idea, even the ones he knew were wrong.
words.ctx: The young prince wanted honest advisers, not {servile} ones; he grew tired of courtiers who said only what he wanted to hear.
words.etym: From Latin servilis, “like a servant,” from servus (servant).

mn.text: Asked to pass the salt, Felix leaps up, polishes the shaker, bows and asks if he may also cut Ada’s food; that overeager serving is {servile}.

scene.alt: A man bows deeply while handing a salt shaker to a puzzled woman at a café table.

words.def: flattering in an overeager, groveling way
words.ex: The {fawning} fans crowded around the singer, praising even her sneezes.
words.ctx: The review was not criticism but {fawning} praise: the writer called every scene a masterpiece and every actor a genius.
words.note: To fawn (to flatter) is a different word from fawn (a baby deer).

mn.text: The puppy wags, rolls over and licks Sven’s boots, all for one biscuit; flattery that eager, from a person, is {fawning}.

scene.alt: A puppy leaps and wags, begging for a treat from a laughing man.

words.ex: The {insolent} student rolled his eyes and yawned loudly while the principal spoke.
words.ctx: Asked politely to wait her turn, the customer was {insolent}: she snapped her fingers at the clerk and demanded the manager at once.
words.etym: From Latin insolens, “unusual, overbearing”: in- (not) + solere (to be used to).

mn.text: Told to tidy his room, teenage Rex crosses his arms and says, “Make me!” Talking back that rudely is {insolent}.

scene.alt: A teen crosses his arms and refuses to clean his messy room as his mother points in shock.

words.ex: The {impudent} parrot squawked “Bad haircut!” at every visitor.
words.ctx: Rather than apologizing for being late, the {impudent} boy grinned and asked why the class had started without him.
words.etym: From Latin impudens, “shameless”: in- (not) + pudens (feeling shame).

mn.text: Rosa’s parrot is a little imp: it squawks “Bad haircut!” at every guest who walks in. The bird is {impudent}.

scene.alt: A cheeky parrot squawks an insult at a bald grandfather, who looks shocked.

words.ex: In a {brazen} move, the squirrel climbed onto the picnic table and grabbed a whole sandwich.
words.ctx: The thief was {brazen}: rather than sneaking in at night, he strolled through the front door at noon and waved at the security camera.
words.etym: From Old English for “made of brass”: a brazen face is as hard and bold as brass.
words.note: To brazen it out is to act boldly, as if one had done nothing wrong.

mn.text: In front of the whole family, the squirrel hops onto the picnic table, grabs a sandwich and stares right back at them; it is as bold as brass, {brazen}.

scene.alt: A bold squirrel stands on a picnic table with a sandwich while a family watches.

words.ex: The rookie had the {temerity} to correct the famous coach in front of the whole team.
words.ctx: Few people dared to argue with the stern old judge, so the courtroom gasped when a young clerk had the {temerity} to point out his mistake.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

words.etym: From Latin temeritas, “rashness,” from temere (blindly, rashly).
words.note: Temerity (nerve) is nearly the opposite of timidity (shyness), though they sound alike.

mn.cue: TEAM-erity: the rookie tells the TEAM captain
mn.text: On her first day, the smallest player on the team tells the giant captain, “You’re doing it wrong!” Everyone gasps at her {temerity}.

scene.alt: A small new player points up at the huge team captain and tells him he is wrong while a teammate gasps.

words.def: shameless boldness; the nerve to do something rude
words.ex: After breaking our window, he had the {effrontery} to ask for his ball back.
words.ctx: The guest ate most of the cake before the birthday girl could blow out her candles, then had the {effrontery} to complain that it was too sweet.
words.etym: From French effronterie, from Late Latin effrons, “shameless, barefaced”: ex- (out) + frons (forehead, face).

mn.text: Rex strolls past the long line, steps right to the front of it and tells the clerk to hurry up; that shameless nerve is {effrontery}.

scene.alt: A man cuts to the front of a long line and shouts at the clerk while the others glare.

after.cap: Bowing and boldness, from polite to rude.

after.html: Temerity (nerve) and timidity (shyness) sound alike but are nearly opposites. And the verb fawn (to flatter) has nothing to do with a fawn, a baby deer.

items.q: Which word describes proper, polite respect rather than too much?
items.why: Deferential means showing polite respect. The others mean too eager to please.

items.q: “He had the ______ to call the champion a beginner.” Which word fits?
items.why: Temerity is reckless boldness, nerve. Timidity is shyness, nearly the opposite.
pudere means to feel shame; im- (not) + pud: an impudent person feels no shame.

items.q: Which word names a person, not a quality?
items.why: A sycophant is a flatterer. The other three are adjectives.
